entries.section: (1) The emigration of Elimelech

paragraphs.text: The rule of the judges: this is a period of 450 years after the death of Joshua the son of Nun, during which the Jews mixed with the surrounding pagans. God was angry with them, and the pagans occupied them and humiliated them. Then they repented, and God sent them a judge who ruled by His Law and delivered them from their enemies. Then they returned to mixing with the wicked, and God was angry with them a second time, and this story was repeated many times.

A famine: this is the famine that occurred in the days of Gideon (Judg 6:1-6, 11), because the Midianites and the Amalekites plundered the food of the Jews. This was a chastening from God because of their neglect of His Law and their mixing and intermarrying with the pagans.

Bethlehem-Judah: a village located south of Jerusalem at a distance of five miles. It is where Rachel died.. and in it Christ was born later. It was called Bethlehem-Judah because it lies in the portion of the tribe of Judah, to distinguish it from another village called Bethlehem, which lies in the portion of the tribe of Zebulun.
Moab: he was the son of Lot, and the Moabites were a people who troubled the children of Israel, and God commanded them not to mix with them. They lived east of the Jordan River.

In the days of the era of the judges, and specifically in the days of Gideon, a famine occurred in the land of Judah. One of the Jews could not bear it, so he emigrated to the pagan land of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons. This was a wrong act and contrary to the Law of God, for he did not seek God's guidance and went to a pagan people with whom God had commanded them not to mix (Deut 23:3). It was weakness of faith in the power of God, who is able to provide for him in the midst of the famine, especially since this famine was a chastening from God because of their neglect of His Law; it would have been better for him to repent and hold fast to the commandments of God.

If distress comes upon you, return to God with repentance and ask for His help, and do not rely on solving the problem with your material thoughts, lest you move further away from God. And trust that your God loves you and will not leave you in the midst of distress.

entries.section: (1) The emigration of Elimelech

paragraphs.text: Elimelech: a name meaning "my God is king."
Naomi: a name meaning "pleasant of heart."
Mahlon: a name meaning "poverty and sickness."
Chilion: a name meaning "ruin."

Elimelech did not live according to his name, settling in his land and relying on God, but emigrated to the land of the pagans and took with him his wife Naomi, who lived according to her name, that is, she remained holding fast to her fellowship with God even in a foreign land, and all her longings were attached to returning to her country, where God is worshiped in the Tabernacle of Meeting. As for the names of his two sons, they express the bad condition, not only that which faced him in his own country, where there was famine, but even more the hunger and spiritual ruin that faced him in the land of Moab. It would have been better for him to remain in Bethlehem, which means the house of bread, and which signifies the spiritual bread that the children of God receive in their fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (1) The emigration of Elimelech

paragraphs.text: God wanted to show His anger at this spiritually unsound act of emigrating to a land far from Him, whereby life with God becomes difficult. So the head of the family, Elimelech, died at a young age; he did not reach old age and did not enjoy the material goods that he wished to find in Moab, but his life was defiled by the evil surrounding him, and he died quickly.

entries.section: (1) The emigration of Elimelech

paragraphs.text: Orpah: a Moabite name meaning "neck" or "back of the neck."
Ruth: a Moabite name meaning "beautiful."

The two sons of Naomi married two Moabite women, contrary to the Law of God, which commanded keeping away from them (Deut 23:3), and they lived in married life for ten years and had no children by them. Here too God shows His anger at them, and does not give them fruit in a land foreign to the faith, because they left "Ephratah" (which is the old name of Bethlehem), whose meaning is fruit, a symbol of God's blessings to His children who hold fast to the spiritual life with Him. And the number ten signifies a complete period, that is, they did not obtain fruit however many long years they lived far from God.

entries.section: (1) The emigration of Elimelech

paragraphs.text: God's anger reaches its fullness, and the two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, die, and so Naomi was left alone. Perhaps when a person feels loneliness he returns to God and finds his salvation, and this is what actually happened, as we shall see in the following verses, for Naomi thought of returning to her country.

And we notice here that Ruth did not bear children to her first husband, Mahlon, and this signifies the inability of the Law to offer salvation and blessing; but she bore later to Boaz, and from her offspring came Christ, and this signifies the ability of the Church in the New Testament to offer salvation and spiritual children. So Ruth in her former life is a type of the Church of the Old Testament, and then by her marriage to Boaz, of the Church of the New Testament.

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: Daughters-in-law: the daughter-in-law is the wife of the son.

News reached Naomi that the famine had ended in her country, so she thought of returning to Bethlehem, especially since she had become alone after losing her husband and her two sons. So she arose from her house to travel, and her two daughters-in-law went out with her to bid her farewell and to accompany her on the road of the journey.

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: Naomi thanked her two daughters-in-law for bidding her farewell and accompanying her some distance on the road of the journey, and with kindness and motherliness she asked them to be content with this distance and to return to the city.

And this shows, as will come in the following verses, that Naomi was distinguished by an overflowing love and motherliness that made her two daughters-in-law love her and cling to her. There was no human jealousy or attempt at domination in her fellowship with her daughters-in-law, so she was an example of a spiritual mother-in-law, that is, like a second mother. And Naomi asked God for blessings for them in appreciation of their love for her and for their husbands who had died. For Naomi appreciates feelings of love and gives thanks for them, and even asks God for blessings for those who love.

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: Naomi wished a happy marriage for her daughters-in-law, and this also shows her unselfishness in not refusing the marriage of her daughters-in-law to other husbands after her sons, for her motherliness seeks first the comfort of her daughters-in-law. And before this love between Naomi and her daughters-in-law, the feelings of all were moved and tears overflowed, and the sound of their weeping even rose.

The more love you offer to others, the more you win their souls, so that they want to cling to you, and consequently they learn from you the love of God and you guide them easily to the way of truth, even without words.

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: Her two daughters-in-law showed their attachment to her and declared that they would not leave her but would accompany her to live with her in her country. And this shows how great their love for her was, because she had first offered a great love that they had not heard of nor found among their own people. Thus the children of God appear different from the people of the world.

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: With love Naomi refused that they should accompany her, because she would not be able to provide husbands for them, for she was not pregnant, nor was it expected that she would bear sons who would grow up and marry them.

And Naomi here also, like Ruth in her first life, signifies the inability of the Law to offer salvation and sons and fruits. And she refers here to a practice of the Jews, that if someone died and had no children, his brother would marry his wife, and the firstborn son who was born would be reckoned to the deceased husband (Deut 25:5, 6).

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: The hand of the Lord is gone out against me: that is, He permitted my afflictions, which are the death of my husband and my two sons.

Naomi added that she had grown so old that it would not allow her a second marriage, and the hope that she would bear sons at this age was weak, and consequently she would not be able to provide husbands for them one day. Then she said that if it were possible for her to conceive sons, which is an impossible supposition, a problem would still remain: would her daughters-in-law wait many long years until the sons grew up and there was an opportunity for Orpah and Ruth to marry them?...! This of course is a very slight possibility. For all this she forgot her own need for her daughters-in-law to accompany her and thought of their comfort before her own.

entries.section: (2) The return of Orpah

paragraphs.text: Orpah was persuaded by her mother-in-law's words, so she kissed her and wept much and bade her farewell and returned to her city; but Ruth refused to bid her farewell and clung to her.

And here we find Orpah an example of human love, which appreciates the love of others but has limits, namely human reasoning, so she was persuaded and returned to her house. And so her name indicates this, for the name Orpah means the neck or the back of the neck, that is, she turned her back to her mother-in-law and went back to her place. But Ruth represents the divine love that God gives to His children, which surpasses human love and all reasoning, so she remained clinging to her mother-in-law.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: Sister-in-law: the wife of the husband's brother.

In love and concern from Naomi for Ruth, she tried to prevent her from continuing the journey with her and asked her to return to her country and her gods like her sister-in-law Orpah. For although Naomi needed support because of her old age, she thought of Ruth's comfort before her own.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: The LORD do so to me, and more also: a form of oath meaning that if I go back on my oath, I deserve a punishment greater than the ordinary.

The brilliance of Ruth's love for her mother-in-law appears, for she asked her not to repeat her pity for her and her invitation to return to her people, because Ruth's love surpassed all human love, and this appears in the following:
1- Her clinging to her mother-in-law in her journey and in her dwelling in any place she chooses.
2- Her acceptance to join the people of God and to leave the pagan people of Moab, that is, her desire to become a Jewess, having been influenced by the qualities of her mother-in-law and her faith.
3- Her declaration of her faith in God and her leaving the pagan gods that the Moabites worship.
4- Her insistence on being with her mother-in-law throughout her life, that is, until death, so that nothing can separate her from her mother-in-law except when God wills and one of them dies.

5- Her hope in the eternal life that her mother-in-law hoped for, for even after death she wants to remain with her mother-in-law, so she asks to be buried in the place where her mother-in-law is buried.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: Before the greatness of Ruth's love and her insistence on clinging to her mother-in-law, Naomi fell silent and no longer asked her to return to her country. And her heart was of course filled with joy, for she loved Ruth, so she rejoiced in her constant fellowship and in her acceptance to join the people of God and to believe in Him.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: Naomi continued on the road, with Ruth accompanying her, until they reached Bethlehem, and when they entered the village after an absence of more than ten years, the whole village took an interest in welcoming Naomi, and this shows the following:
1- The standing of Naomi as a devout person beloved by her relatives and neighbors.

2- The change in Naomi's condition: she had gone out with three men, her husband and her two sons, and now she returns alone, accompanied by a young woman of a foreign race, and she has no possessions, whether cattle or anything else, that is, she gained nothing from her emigration but returned in a worse condition than she had been, so she deserved the pity and sorrow of the people of her village.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: Naomi said to those of the village who met her, expressing her sorrow, that they should no longer call her Naomi but Mara, because God had permitted her to be chastened by her leaving her country, so many distresses came upon her, and this is their result, her return alone and poor... So she submits to God and to His chastenings, but she describes her state and her soul as bearing severe distresses.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: Naomi continued her words and said that she went out from here to Moab and was full, for she had a husband and two sons, and now she returns empty after their death. And in faith she accepts the chastening of God, who humbled her and broke her, because she did not believe that she could live with Him and worship Him among her own people and sought material goods, and so she lost everything.

entries.section: (3) Naomi and Ruth in Bethlehem

paragraphs.text: The Holy Bible specifies the time of the return of Naomi and Ruth to Bethlehem, which was the days of the barley harvest, which falls in the end of March and the beginning of April. And this was by the providence of God, who permitted a chastening for Naomi and Ruth but receives them with good among His people, because the days of harvest are wealth and good for the rich, and they also give to the poor who glean behind the reapers. And this was the beginning of the divine blessings for this sorrowful family, and other blessings followed after it until they were completed by the marriage of Ruth to Boaz, the great man, so that by her marriage she became the grandmother of Christ.

If God permits distresses for you, accept them with submission, and then, when God sees your obedience and your humility and your return to Him, He will pour out on you blessings you do not expect, and you will be compensated for all that you lost.
Ruth in the field of Boaz

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: This verse speaks about an important figure in this book, a man called Boaz, whose name means "mighty one." He is indeed a rich man of great standing in his town, strong in his position. And he was a relative of Elimelech, Naomi's husband. He is a type of Christ, who is able to do all things and supports His children however weak they are, and His heart is open with love to all, Jews and Gentiles, just as Boaz received in his field the poor of his own town and Ruth the Gentile.

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: Ruth heard from Naomi her mother-in-law about the Law of the Jews, which is that at their harvest, or the gathering of their produce, if some ears fell from the reapers during the harvest, they would leave them for the poor, who glean behind them to supply their needs (Deut 24:19-22; Lev 19:9, 10; 23:22). So she asked her mother-in-law to permit her to go and gather ears of barley behind the reapers, and she permitted her. And this shows two things:
1- Ruth's diligence and her concern to work to find her sustenance and the sustenance of her mother-in-law.

2- Her humility and good manners, for she asks permission of her mother-in-law in every work even though it is a good work and she takes responsibility from her to meet her needs and those of her mother-in-law.

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: Ruth went to search in the village for a barley field to glean behind the reapers, and God's providence led her to the field of Boaz, a relative of her husband.

God awaits your concern and diligence in order to help you with His grace and His providence until you find your salvation, for He rejoices in your striving and the intention of your heart and rewards you with many blessings.

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: Here the character of Boaz appears as a man who manages his properties with care and diligence, so he went out from his house to his fields to inspect the work of the harvest himself. And his kindness and love appear in his greeting to the reapers with a spiritual phrase, saying "The LORD be with you," that is, may God help you in your work and bless you. And the Church still uses this phrase in the Divine Liturgy, and the priest calls it out to the people, and they answer him just as the reapers answered Boaz, for they also said to him a beautiful spiritual phrase, "The LORD bless thee," that is, just as he wished for them the blessing of God, so they also return the greeting to him by wishing the blessing of God as well.

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: This verse shows Boaz's exactness in following up his work, for he had appointed a man in charge on his behalf to oversee the reapers in the field, and he followed with his eyes the reapers as they reaped and also the poor who glean behind them. And his attention was caught by a young woman who was a stranger to the town, for her clothes may have been different in addition to her appearance, so he asked his servant "Whose damsel is this?", that is, to which family does she belong; because a young woman is ascribed to her husband or her father or her master.

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: His servant told him that she was the Moabite damsel who had come back with Naomi, because the news had spread throughout all Bethlehem of Ruth's love and sincerity. And he called her a damsel because of her young age.

entries.section: (1) Ruth gleans in the field

paragraphs.text: The house: a tent that they make in the field so that the workers may rest in it from the heat of the day. It may also be meant the house of Naomi.

The servant continued his words and said that Ruth came in the morning and asked permission to glean behind the reapers, and when they noticed her diligence and good manners, they also permitted her to glean among the sheaves that they were gathering to one side, from which some ears would fall, because the one who gleans must be trustworthy, or else she would take from the sheaves themselves. And this makes clear that Ruth had found grace in the eyes of the servant and the reapers, so they permitted her to do this. And her diligence also appears in that she was working all the time and rested only a little in the house, which was most likely a tent set up in the field.

And Ruth signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which sought Christ to find her salvation, and responded to His call and strove and so excelled over the Church of the Jews, which Naomi signifies, for she remained in the house because of her weakness. And the Church of the Gentiles found grace in the eyes of Christ and His servants.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: Hearest thou not, my daughter: a phrase meaning, listen attentively, my daughter.

The fatherhood of Boaz and his care appear in his concern for Ruth, for he called her and said to her, listen, my daughter, for she had changed from a stranger into a beloved daughter.. this is the grace of God given to His striving children. And he welcomed her to glean in his fields and even insisted that she not go to another field, lest anyone trouble her. And he charged his servants to take care of her and not to harm her, so he regarded her as one of the young women known to him and permitted to glean behind the reapers. And his tenderness also appears in that he permitted her to drink from the vessels of water from which the reapers drink if they thirst during the work in the heat of the day.
And the vessels of water signify the Church, from which the Holy Spirit overflows upon all who labor in the field of service and spiritual striving.
And Ruth's keeping close to the young women of Boaz signifies the spiritual person's sharing with his brethren in the Church in their spiritual striving, so that he is encouraged by them.
And the good treatment of Ruth by Boaz is due to:
1- That he is a devout man who carries out the commandment of the Law concerning hospitality to strangers (Ex 23:9; Lev 19:33, 34).
2- That he heard of her love and sincerity toward her mother-in-law and then her going out to work to meet her needs and those of her mother-in-law.
3- That she is his relative through her husband.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: Ruth marveled at this good treatment with which Boaz treated her, for she had not found the like of it in Moab in the way the people of the land treat strangers, so she bowed before him in appreciation of his love and said to him, what is this great grace that I have found in thine eyes.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: When Boaz saw her humility and her appreciation of his love, he praised her for the following:
1- Her sincerity and love in accompanying her mother-in-law and caring for her.
2- Her leaving her father and mother and her people to live among a people foreign to her for the sake of caring for her mother-in-law and enjoying her fellowship.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: Boaz continues his praise of Ruth for her leaving her pagan gods and her taking refuge in God, in whom she believed, to be sheltered under His care, so he asks God to give her the reward for this faith, which is the enjoyment of fellowship with God in addition to all the material blessings on earth.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: Ruth thanked Boaz for his love and asked him to continue this grace for her, and declared that she had received great comfort through his love for her, which supported her in her trial, for she had lost her husband and lives in a foreign country and lives as a poor woman. And in humility she asked to be a handmaid to him, although she is a person of standing in her own country, but this is the humility that moves hearts with love toward the humble.

The more you humble yourself before people and thank them for their kindnesses and appreciate all their good works, the more you win their hearts and receive blessings from God and abundant love from people.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: Vinegar: it is what is mixed with olive oil and resembles a salad.
Parched corn: tender grains of wheat that are roasted and then eaten either raw or cooked.

Boaz continued honoring Ruth, so he regarded her as one of the reapers working for him, and invited her at mealtime to eat bread with them and to dip it also in the vinegar, and he also gave her plenty of parched corn, and she ate and had some left.

entries.section: (2) The dialogue of Boaz with Ruth

paragraphs.text: Sheaves: the bundles.
Let fall: leave some ears to fall from the sheaves you have gathered as if they had fallen by accident on the ground, so that they would not embarrass Ruth.

After Ruth ate, she arose with diligence to continue her gleaning of the ears behind the reapers and also among the sheaves that they had gathered to one side, for Boaz and his reapers trusted in her faithfulness, and with love Boaz wanted to give her more ears, and so as not to embarrass her he told his reapers that when she walked behind them they should draw out some ears from the sheaves they were gathering and leave them to fall on the ground as if they had fallen by accident so that Ruth might gather more ears... It was a wonderful gentleness of feeling by which Boaz was distinguished.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: Beat out: she struck the ears of wheat with a rod and separated the grain from the straw.
Ephah: a measure holding 22.9 liters, equal to about 17 kg of wheat.

Ruth continued gleaning the ears with diligence until evening, that is, the end of the day, and she gathered many ears, which she beat out and separated their grain alone, and the amount of grain was about an ephah of barley, which is a large amount that an ordinary young woman could not glean in a day, but it was the blessing of God and the generosity of Boaz. And this amount of barley is enough for the sustenance of Ruth and her mother-in-law for many days.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: Ruth hurried to her mother-in-law's house to give her the barley she had gathered and also to give her some of what was left over after she had eaten of the parched corn and the bread. It is the feelings of love that do not want to eat alone but must share with her mother-in-law in what she eats.

May you feel for those around you, the members of your household and the poor, and let them enjoy what you enjoy, not only of material things, but also share with them what you enjoy of spiritual things, so that you tell them what you have heard about God and encourage them to be bound to the Church.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: When Naomi saw the features of joy on Ruth's face and the good that she had brought from the field, she asked her about the field in which she had gleaned, and she blessed whoever met her while she was gleaning, because she rejoiced at the sight of her and at the good that was with her. So Ruth answered that she had gleaned in the field of a man called Boaz.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: The kinsman: the nearest person to the deceased, who has the right to pay what is owed on the deceased's fields as a pledge, to restore his inheritance to him, and to marry his wife in order to raise up offspring in his name.

Naomi rejoiced that Ruth had gleaned in the field of Boaz and asked a blessing for him from God after she learned from Ruth all that he had honored her with, and she praised him because he had shown kindness to the living, namely Naomi and Ruth, and to the dead, namely Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion, for his honoring Ruth is an honoring of Naomi and of her husband and her two sons who had died. And by this Naomi's appreciation of kindness and her thanks for it appear. Then she informed Ruth that Boaz is their second kinsman, that is, there is a kinsman nearer than he to Ruth, and then Boaz is the second kinsman.
And the first kinsman signifies the Law, which is unable to redeem us (as will become clear in ch. 4), while the second kinsman, that is, Boaz, signifies Christ, who redeemed us on the Cross.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: Ruth also told Naomi about the good treatment of Boaz toward her, for he had invited her to continue gleaning grain in his fields until the end of the harvest, not only the barley harvest but also the wheat harvest that follows it.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: Naomi rejoiced at this welcome from Boaz and urged Ruth to stay in his fields so as to find this good treatment and so that no one would harm her in strange fields.

entries.section: (3) Ruth in the house of Naomi

paragraphs.text: Ruth obeyed with joy and continued gleaning the ears throughout the period of the barley and wheat harvest, and she would bring all that she gathered to her mother-in-law and take care of serving her.
Ruth is an example of perseverance, diligence, love and service to others. And she signifies those who strive spiritually throughout their lives until they attain the Kingdom.
Ruth at the threshing floor of Boaz

entries.section: (1) Naomi's counsel to Ruth

paragraphs.text: Although Naomi found her sustenance from Ruth's labor in gathering ears every day, which sufficed her and was more than enough, yet in love she wanted stability and a better life for Ruth, and she told her so.

entries.section: (1) Naomi's counsel to Ruth

paragraphs.text: Winnoweth: the process of winnowing is the separation of the grains of barley from the straw.
Threshingfloor: a wide place where the processes of threshing and winnowing are carried out to separate the grain from the straw, and then the grain is gathered into the storehouse.

Naomi reminded Ruth that Boaz is a relative of hers through her husband, and consequently he could marry her and she would settle into a happy life. And the day is suitable for meeting him, because it is a day of joy with the winnowing and gathering of the barley crop on the threshingfloor. And the relative is the kinsman whom the Law calls to marry the wife of the deceased, and the firstborn son is reckoned to the deceased, and thereby he raises up offspring for him (Deut 25:5-10).

entries.section: (1) Naomi's counsel to Ruth

paragraphs.text: Naomi asked Ruth to take off the clothes of her widowhood and to prepare to be in the most beautiful appearance by washing and anointing herself with perfumes and putting on the best she had, then to go to the threshingfloor of Boaz but to hide herself so that no one would know of her presence, and to watch him from afar until he had finished eating and drinking, that is, had taken his supper, before he lay down.

And Ruth's preparation to be like a bride for Boaz signifies the preparation of the human soul that wants to enjoy Christ: it must wash, that is, receive the sacrament of Baptism, and then be anointed, that is, receive the sacrament of the Holy Myron with the holy oil. And after it receives the new nature and the Holy Spirit dwells in it, it puts on the garments of righteousness, that is, puts on Christ, and then it can be before Him on the threshingfloor, where the grain is separated from the straw, which signifies the Day of Judgment. But because the soul is prepared, it rejoices in this day when it meets its Bridegroom, who judges the world, and He takes it to be His bride. This Bridegroom is Christ, whom Boaz signifies.

entries.section: (1) Naomi's counsel to Ruth

paragraphs.text: She said to her, notice the place where he goes and sleeps, and after making sure that he is asleep, go and lie down at his feet. And this practice was well known, for slaves and maidservants used to sleep at the feet of their masters so as to serve them if they wished during the night. In addition, Ruth is a devout person and Boaz likewise a righteous man, and the purpose of Ruth's act was that Boaz might feel his responsibility and his duty as kinsman toward her so as to marry her, and not any lustful purpose, especially since the difference in age was great between the young woman Ruth and the older man Boaz.

entries.section: (1) Naomi's counsel to Ruth

paragraphs.text: Ruth's obedience to Naomi appears, although the words of the Jewish Law were new to her, but in confidence in her mother-in-law's love for her she obeyed, bearing any risks that might meet her or any bad treatment that she might face.

May you think of the comfort of those around you before your own comfort, and if you accustom yourself to this in your youth, you can keep the spirit of giving and sacrifice however old you grow and become needy and weak, and you will continue to think of what to give your strong children, and then you will experience the mercies of God and His countless gifts.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: The heap of corn: heaps of sheaves of barley stored at the edge of the threshingfloor.

Ruth obeyed all of Naomi's words and went to the threshingfloor of Boaz, and after he finished eating and drinking, and his heart was of course glad at the new harvest, he went to sleep in a tent or small hut that had been made for him beside the heaps of sheaves of barley at the side of the threshingfloor. And after he had fallen deeply asleep and the workers on the threshingfloor had also slept, Ruth slipped in quietly and uncovered his feet and lay down and covered herself with the edge of his covering, to declare to him that just as his feet were uncovered of the covering, so she too needs someone to cover her and marry her and carry out the commandment of the Jewish Law and raise up offspring for her dead husband.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: Spread therefore thy skirt: cover me with the edge of your garment, that is, offer me your care and your protection and your covering by marrying me, so as to carry out the Law and raise up offspring for my dead husband.

In the middle of the night Boaz turned in his sleep and felt the presence of someone at his feet, so he was startled and asked, who is sleeping at my feet?.. So Ruth, who had been awake all night, hurried, and perhaps she had been praying during these hours that God would prosper her way and give her grace in the eyes of Boaz so that he would not rebuke her or reject her, and she answered him that she was Ruth his handmaid, and asked him to cover her as a kinsman and marry her and care for her in order to raise up offspring for her dead husband. And this action shows many virtues in Ruth, namely:
1- Her obedience to her mother-in-law despite the difficulty of the responsibility.
2- Her humility in saying that she was his handmaid.
3- Her courage in facing this difficult situation
4- Her love of God and obedience to His Law, so she set aside every earthly desire to marry a young man and asked for the carrying out of the word of God.
And Ruth signifies the soul that is alone with Christ in the night to pray and to contemplate His beauty and to ask for His care for it and its union with Him in love.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: Boaz praised her for two things:
1- Her first kindness, which was her leaving her family and her people and her gods to accompany her mother-in-law and embrace her religion and live among her people.

2- Her second kindness, which is the greater, by which she wanted to raise up offspring for her dead husband by marrying an old man, Boaz, and she was not preoccupied with young men, poor or rich, to satisfy her human desires.

Be occupied with the love of God and His commandments, and you will enjoy fellowship with Him before you seek your material needs and your lawful desires, because the love of God satisfies the soul, and He then provides for all the needs of the body.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: The gate of my people: that is, all the families living in houses that have doors, and it means all the people of the city.

Boaz then reassured Ruth that he had the right of kinsmanship and care for her, and praised her as a virtuous woman, and all the people of the city agree on this because of what she did for her mother-in-law.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: Boaz informed Ruth that he is a kinsman and ready to perform the right of a kinsman, but there is a kinsman nearer than he. And this shows Boaz's carefulness in carrying out the Law of God, for he did not use his influence to achieve what he was convinced of, for he is also a devout man who knows how to carry out the Law.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: Boaz permitted Ruth to stay the night on the threshingfloor until morning because she could not return to her house during the night, and in the morning Boaz would summon the nearer kinsman to do his duty and marry Ruth and redeem the field of Elimelech her father-in-law, which was mortgaged, which he had mortgaged because of his poverty before he emigrated to Moab (ch. 4:3, 4). And Boaz confirmed his words with an oath, which was well known at that time, namely "as the LORD liveth," that he would fulfill this matter and summon the nearer kinsman, and if he did not perform his duties, he himself would perform the right of a kinsman.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: Ruth lay at the side of the threshingfloor until morning, and at the beginning of dawn, before anyone could distinguish from afar the features of any person, Boaz called her to return to her house, and out of respect for her standing he said to her, let no one know that you came to the threshingfloor, so that it might be clear that he is the one who performed the right of a kinsman of his own accord, although it would not have been wrong for her to demand her right, but he tried to give her a better standing, and on the other hand so that no one would think that there was some shameful act between a man and a woman, although the piety of Boaz and Ruth is evident, yet he is careful in everything. And his private servant may have awakened, and Boaz informed him not to tell anyone of the coming of a woman to the threshingfloor.

entries.section: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

paragraphs.text: Before Ruth departed, Boaz wanted to honor her, so he asked her to bring her outer garment, which is like a cloak or a wrap that is wrapped over the clothes, and then he put in it six measures of barley. And what is meant by this measure is most likely the omer, which equals about 1.75 kg, that is, he gave her about 10.5 kg of grains of barley, and she tied it up in this garment, and then Boaz helped her tenderly and placed it on her shoulders for her to return with it to her mother-in-law. And Ruth departed, returning to Naomi, and then a little later Boaz also arose and entered the city to summon the kinsman and come to an understanding with him.

entries.section: (3) Ruth's return to Naomi

paragraphs.text: Ruth reached her mother-in-law's house at the beginning of dawn, and her mother-in-law was deeply asleep, so when she heard knocking on the door and the voice of a woman speaking to her, she asked her who she was, because she had not yet fully awakened from her sleep. So she told her that she was Ruth, and then she hurried to open to her, and Ruth entered and told her everything that had happened in detail.

entries.section: (3) Ruth's return to Naomi

paragraphs.text: Ruth also told her mother-in-law of the generosity of Boaz, who gave her a large quantity of barley.

entries.section: (3) Ruth's return to Naomi

paragraphs.text: Naomi was confident of the love of God and the nobility and piety of Boaz, so she reassured Ruth, saying to her, sit still and rest, for God will provide good, and the devout Boaz will not rest until he has completed your marriage.

In the most difficult situations be assured that God provides good for you however adverse matters may seem, for He turns them to your good and will not neglect you until you feel rest and peace in His hands.
The marriage of Ruth

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: It appears that the gate of the city of Bethlehem was higher than the rest of the city, so Boaz went up to it. And at the gate there is a square where the leaders of the people sit to judge the affairs of the city, and there the men of the city pass by to go out to their work. So out of Boaz's concern to complete the matter for Ruth, he went there early.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: The Law provides that every word shall be established at the mouth of two or three witnesses (Deut 17:6), but Boaz here called a larger number to confirm and establish what was done, and the number ten also indicates completeness. And he called them from among the elders whose opinion is respected in the matters concerning the city.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: When a famine occurred in Bethlehem and Elimelech became poor, he mortgaged his land for a sum of money to provide for his material needs; then he traveled to Moab, and with his death and the death of his two sons his land became the property of his wife Naomi and the wife of his son, Ruth, because Orpah, the wife of the second son, remained in Moab and perhaps she had married one of the pagans of her people in her country. Therefore Ruth sells her land, meaning she needs someone to pay the mortgage and recover the land of her husband and her father-in-law.

And two things were required, the first the redeeming of the land and the second marriage to Ruth. And Boaz began by presenting the first matter to the kinsman before the elders, which was the redeeming of the land, and afterward he would present to him the second requirement.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: Boaz and the kinsman and the ten elders sat in the square in front of the gate of the city, and others of the people came to this presentation of the case, and Boaz asked the kinsman nearer to Ruth to redeem her land, that is, to pay the price of the mortgage and restore the land, and if he could not, then Boaz is the second kinsman and he is ready to redeem the land. So the first kinsman answered, declaring his agreement to redeem the land, and his purpose in this was to enlarge his properties so as to use this land to increase his production and his wealth.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: After the first kinsman agreed to redeem the land, Boaz asked of him the second requirement, which is linked to the first, namely marriage to Ruth so that he might raise up by her offspring ascribed to her husband and her father-in-law, and in this way the name and inheritance of Elimelech would not be cut off in Israel.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: The first kinsman refused to redeem the land when he found himself obliged to marry Ruth, and he stated that the reason is that by redeeming the land he would mar his own inheritance. He means that he would buy a land, paying the price of its mortgage, and then it would become the property of Ruth's son, and his other sons would take nothing from it, because the man was married and had sons. So he would pay money and then the inheritance would pass to his son by Ruth who would be ascribed to Elimelech. In this he did not think of fulfilling the Law by raising up a son for his dead relative, but thought only of his possessions, and did not want to spend money or effort from which he would not reap an inheritance for his children, because his new son by Ruth would be ascribed to Elimelech. So it is clear that he loves money more than he loves fulfilling the Law and helping others. And in the end he said to Boaz, redeem for yourself the land of Elimelech and marry Ruth, for I will not marry her.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: The Law provided in (Deut 25:7-10) that the kinsman who refuses to marry the wife of the dead man to raise up offspring for him is to take off his sandal and give it to the kinsman who follows him, as a declaration of his giving up his responsibility. And the taking off of the sandal signifies the inability of this kinsman, who takes off the sandal, to tread on the land of the deceased, which he refused to buy, leaving the next kinsman after him to redeem the land and tread on it. Therefore Moses took off his sandal before God in the bush, and the priests and deacons take off their sandals when they enter the sanctuary, to declare that they are not the true Bridegroom, but Christ is the Good Shepherd and they are His servants. For He is the true Kinsman of our souls, who bought us with His blood on the Cross, and it is He who brings us into our new land, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, and He bought it and prepared it for us and entered it after He completed our redemption to declare that we have entry into it through our faith and our life with Him.

entries.section: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

paragraphs.text: The first kinsman declared his refusal to redeem the land and marry Ruth, so he took off his sandal before the elders as the Law provides, and by this declaration it became Boaz's right to marry Ruth and redeem the land. And Boaz here signifies Christ, who marries His Church and raises up from her many children, and redeems, that is, pays all the debts of sin, for His bride.
Do not be occupied with the love of money, because it passes away, but use it to win the love of others and to show mercy to the needy, for this is what remains to you and with it you enter eternity.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Boaz to Ruth

paragraphs.text: Boaz affirmed before the elders and all who were gathered at the gate of the city that he now had the right of kinsmanship over Ruth, since the first kinsman had given it up, so he can now redeem the land.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Boaz to Ruth

paragraphs.text: The gate of his place: it means the gate of the city of Bethlehem, that is, the name of Elimelech will be remembered in Bethlehem because he has offspring.
Likewise it is Boaz's right to marry Ruth and raise up offspring by her, so that the memory of Elimelech may not be cut off in Israel.

So that no misunderstanding occurs between you and others, when you agree on something, may you confirm it in specific and clear words. That is, be exact in your speech and specific so as to keep your peace with others.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Boaz to Ruth

paragraphs.text: The elders and those present declared their agreement that Boaz should become the kinsman able to marry Ruth and redeem the land, and that they were witnesses to this agreement, and they even declared their wishes and good prayer for him that Ruth would be to Boaz like Leah and Rachel, by whom the people of the children of Israel were formed. That is, they wished for him good, blessed offspring from Ruth, and they also prayed for him to have strength in his spiritual and social life, which would appear in his city Ephratah, which is Bethlehem.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of Boaz to Ruth

paragraphs.text: The elders also prayed for Boaz for strength and blessing like Pharez, who broke forth against Zarah his brother at their birth (Gen 38), and had strong offspring, and from him came Boaz. And this Pharez was the son of Judah by Tamar.

entries.section: (3) David from the offspring of Ruth

paragraphs.text: After Boaz became the kinsman responsible for Ruth, he married her, and the blessing of God appeared for this person of foreign race whose heart was filled with love and faith in God and His Law, so He granted her to conceive and bear a son, and she called him Obed (v. 17). And here the emphasis is on Ruth, although Boaz too rejoiced in the grace of God in this newborn, because the son would be ascribed to Mahlon, the deceased husband of Ruth, and to his grandfather Elimelech.

The blessings of God are many for the weak who believe in Him and cry out to Him because they have no one but Him. So hold fast to God however difficult your circumstances, and trust that He will not leave you, but on the contrary He esteems all the works of your love and rewards you with blessings on earth and in heaven.

entries.section: (3) David from the offspring of Ruth

paragraphs.text: Not only did Ruth and Boaz rejoice in the newborn, but Naomi also rejoiced in him greatly, and the women of Bethlehem rejoiced with her, so they hurried to congratulate her on the newborn, whom they called "a kinsman," because through him the name of his father Mahlon and his grandfather Elimelech and also his grandmother Naomi would be remembered.

entries.section: (3) David from the offspring of Ruth

paragraphs.text: The women praised the newborn and told Naomi that through him her soul would be refreshed and rejoice, for through him she would have offspring and a name in Israel. And also when he grows up and Naomi becomes old, he will care for her and her need in her old age. And they praised Ruth, for they told Naomi that Ruth's love and care for her is better than having seven sons, who would not care for her as Ruth tends her and loves her, and consequently she should not grieve over the loss of her husband and her two sons, because Ruth has compensated her for them.

entries.section: (3) David from the offspring of Ruth

paragraphs.text: In the tenderness of motherhood, Naomi embraced the newborn and took care of his upbringing with his mother Ruth, and Naomi's neighbors shared her joy and chose a name for the newborn, "Obed," which means servant, that is, servant of God. Thus they wished that he would live in obedience to God as His servant and gladden the heart of his mother and father and grandmother. And the book mentions that Obed is the father of Jesse and the grandfather of David the prophet, from whom came Christ the Savior of the world.

And Obed signifies Christ, who humbled Himself by His Incarnation, taking the form of a servant to complete our redemption, and just as Ruth contained him in her womb, so Naomi took him in her arms. Thus everyone who receives Christ within him obtains salvation and joy, whether he is from the Jews or from the Gentiles, for He is the Savior of the whole world.

entries.section: (3) David from the offspring of Ruth

paragraphs.text: Pharez: he is the son of Judah the son of Jacob, whom he begot by Tamar (Gen 38). Hezron: a large clan came out of him (Gen 46:12; Num 26:6). Ram: he is Aram as mentioned in (Mt 1:3). Amminadab: he is the father of Elisheba the wife of Aaron (Ex 6:23). Nahshon: he is the brother of Elisheba the wife of Aaron and was the prince of the tribe of Judah in the days of Moses the prophet (Num 2:3, 10:14).
Salmon: one of the great men of Judah in the days of Joshua the son of Nun, and he married Rahab, who received the spies in Jericho.

And the rest of the names mentioned are well known and have been mentioned before, for these very names were mentioned in the genealogy of Christ in (Mt 1), and it may be that some names were omitted from this genealogy because of their little importance, or it may be that there are no omitted names.

And although the book began with a distress, which is the famine because of which Elimelech emigrated to Moab, it ends with happy news, which is the birth of Obed, from whose offspring came Christ, the Bread of Life and the Savior of the world. And this genealogy also shows the love of Christ and His humility, who came from the offspring of Ruth the Moabitess, and even from the offspring of Gentile women and even harlots like Rahab, for He honors women in general, since He mentioned in His genealogy all these, that is, Tamar and Ruth and Rahab, the Gentile women, in addition to Bathsheba, the Jewish wife of David, with whom he committed adultery. For Christ came to save the whole world, Jews and Gentiles, and to turn sinners into saints.
